content: In the 19th century, the term midget was used in medical contexts to describe individuals who were extremely short but had body proportions that were considered normal. This term was contrasted with dwarf, which referred to individuals with disproportionate short stature. Over time, as the term midget entered common language, it was often used in a derogatory manner. Today, when used to describe a very short person, the term midget is widely regarded as offensive and is considered an example of the euphemism treadmill, where terms evolve to avoid negative connotations. The term dwarf has largely replaced midget in reference to proportionally short individuals, though the term little person is now the preferred terminology. According to the organization Little People of America, dwarfism is defined as a medical or genetic condition that typically results in an adult height of 4'10 (147 cm) or shorter in both men and women, although in some cases, individuals with a dwarfing condition may be slightly taller than this threshold. Modern medical terminology distinguishes between two types of dwarfism: proportionate dwarfism and disproportionate dwarfism. Proportionate dwarfism, such as primordial dwarfism, refers to individuals whose body proportions are normal but are uniformly small. Disproportionate dwarfism, such as achondroplasia, involves individuals with abnormal body proportions, often with shorter limbs relative to the trunk. Proportionate dwarfism is frequently caused by hormonal deficiencies, such as a lack of human growth hormone, and in some cases, it can be treated medically.
